clinicalPearls: Eight filarial species infect humans, but four cause most symptomatic disease: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Onchocerca volvulus, and Loa loa (Harrison 22e p.1819).

Filarial disease is characteristically more acute and intense in newly exposed travelers/transmigrants than in lifelong natives of endemic areas; infection usually requires repeated, prolonged exposure to infective larvae (Harrison 22e p.1819).

Lymphatic filariasis (W. bancrofti, B. malayi, B. timori) is widely distributed; W. bancrofti affects ~51 million people and B. malayi occurs primarily in eastern India, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines; humans are the only definitive host for W. bancrofti (Harrison 22e p.1819-1820).
Most W. bancrofti is nocturnally periodic (microfilariae scarce by day, increasing at night); blood for microfilaria detection must be timed to the regional periodicity (Harrison 22e p.1819-1821).

Common presentations of lymphatic filariasis are asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema/elephantiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1820).
Genital lymphatic involvement (funiculitis, epididymitis, hydrocele, scrotal elephantiasis) occurs almost exclusively with W. bancrofti, not Brugia (Harrison 22e p.1820).
ADL lymphangitis is retrograde (spreads peripherally from the draining node), a feature that distinguishes filarial lymphangitis from ascending bacterial lymphangitis (Harrison 22e p.1820-1821).

Dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA) presents with fever, chills, myalgias, demarcated edematous plaques, and entry lesions (often interdigital) and is frequently misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820).
Obstruction of retroperitoneal lymphatics can rupture renal lymphatics and produce intermittent chyluria, typically most prominent in the morning (Harrison 22e p.1820).

On high-frequency ultrasound, live adult worms in dilated lymphatics show a distinctive motion called the 'filarial dance sign'; worms are seen in the spermatic cord in up to 80% of W. bancrofti-infected men (Harrison 22e p.1821).

Circulating antigen assays (ELISA and rapid lateral-flow) for W. bancrofti have sensitivities of 93-100% and specificity approaching 100% and detect both microfilaremic and cryptic amicrofilaremic infection; there is currently NO circulating-antigen test for brugian filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821).

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) presents with nocturnal paroxysmal cough/wheeze, weight loss, low-grade fever, marked blood eosinophilia (>3000/uL), and very high IgE and antifilarial antibody; microfilariae are cleared from blood by the lungs and are typically NOT found in peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.1821-1822).

Onchocerciasis ('river blindness'), caused by O. volvulus, primarily affects skin, eyes, and lymph nodes; pruritus and a generalized papular rash are most common, and visual impairment is the most serious complication (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823).

Sclerosing keratitis (in 1-5% of infected persons) is the leading cause of onchocercal blindness; 'snowflake' punctate keratitis around dying microfilariae is common in younger patients and usually resolves (Harrison 22e p.1823).

Onchocercal lymphadenopathy can produce 'hanging groin'; rarely Nakalanga dwarfism and an association with epilepsy/nodding syndrome are seen; blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.1823).

Loiasis (Loa loa, the African eye worm) is suggested by transient subconjunctival worm migration and episodic Calabar swellings (evanescent angioedema); microfilariae have a diurnal periodicity peaking ~10:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. (Harrison 22e p.1823).
Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial endosymbiont present in Brugia, Wuchereria, Mansonella, and Onchocerca, is a target for antifilarial (anti-Wolbachia) therapy (Harrison 22e p.1819, 1824).
harrison.pathophysiology: Filariae are tissue-dwelling nematodes transmitted by mosquitoes or other arthropods; insect-borne infective larvae mature into adult worms that reside in lymphatics (W. bancrofti, Brugia) or subcutaneous tissue (Loa loa, O. volvulus). Adults release microfilariae that circulate in blood or migrate through skin; adults live many years while microfilariae survive 3-36 months. In lymphatic filariasis, pathology results mainly from inflammatory damage caused by ADULT worms (not microfilariae) in afferent lymphatics, with plasma-cell/eosinophil/macrophage infiltration, lymphatic dilation, valve incompetence, and progressive granulomatous reaction and fibrosis (worsened by worm death) leading to obstruction, lymphedema, and elephantiasis; injury is due both to the worm and to host inflammatory response. In contrast, onchocerciasis pathology is elicited by MICROFILARIAE (not adults), causing chronic dermal inflammation/atrophy/fibrosis, fibrous subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomata) around adults, and corneal neovascularization/scarring and intraocular inflammation leading to blindness. In TPE, microfilariae are trapped and cleared by the lungs, provoking allergic/eosinophilic intra-alveolar inflammation that can progress to interstitial fibrosis. Calabar swellings of loiasis are thought to be a hypersensitivity reaction to adult-worm antigens. The Wolbachia endosymbiont contributes to inflammatory reactions (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823).
additionalDifferentials: Acute adenolymphangitis (ADL) vs thrombophlebitis, bacterial infection, and trauma (Harrison 22e p.1821)
Filarial lymphangitis vs ascending bacterial lymphangitis (distinguished by retrograde evolution) (Harrison 22e p.1821)
Chronic filarial lymphedema vs lymphedema of malignancy, postoperative scarring, trauma, chronic edematous states, and congenital lymphatic abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.1821)
DLA frequently misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820)

TPE vs asthma, Loffler's syndrome, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), other systemic vasculitides (notably periarteritis nodosa), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, and hypereosinophilic syndromes (Harrison 22e p.1822)
infectionMimics: Ascending bacterial lymphangitis (mimics filarial ADL) (Harrison 22e p.1821)
Bacterial cellulitis (DLA is often diagnosed as cellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.1820)
nonInfectiousMimics: Lymphedema of malignancy, postoperative scarring, trauma, chronic edematous states, congenital lymphatic abnormalities (mimic chronic filarial lymphedema) (Harrison 22e p.1821)
Asthma and Loffler's syndrome (mimic TPE) (Harrison 22e p.1822)

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), other systemic vasculitides including periarteritis nodosa, chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, hypereosinophilic syndromes (mimic TPE) (Harrison 22e p.1822)
additionalInvestigations: Microscopy of blood, hydrocele fluid, or other body fluids for microfilariae, with concentration by polycarbonate membrane filtration (3 um pore) or Knott's formalin centrifugation technique; collection timed to microfilarial periodicity (Harrison 22e p.1821)
Circulating filarial antigen assays for W. bancrofti (ELISA and rapid lateral-flow); no antigen test available for brugian filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821)
PCR for W. bancrofti and B. malayi DNA in blood (sensitivity equal to or greater than parasitologic methods) (Harrison 22e p.1821)
High-frequency ultrasound with Doppler of scrotum/lymph nodes/breast to visualize motile adult worms ('filarial dance sign') (Harrison 22e p.1821)
Radionuclide lymphoscintigraphy (mainly a research/lymphedema-assessment tool) (Harrison 22e p.1821)

Eosinophilia, elevated serum IgE, and elevated antifilarial antibody (supportive, with extensive helminth cross-reactivity; W. bancrofti- and B. malayi-specific antigen serology has specificity >98%) (Harrison 22e p.1821)
Skin snip (incubated in saline/medium; microfilariae emerge in 2-4 h or overnight) or excised nodule for onchocerciasis; Onchocerca-specific antibody assays (Harrison 22e p.1823)
Chest x-ray/CT and pulmonary function tests in TPE (restrictive in most, obstructive in half) (Harrison 22e p.1822)
Detection of L. loa microfilariae in blood, removal of adult worm from eye/subcutaneous biopsy, or PCR/recombinant-antigen serology for loiasis (Harrison 22e p.1823)
redFlags: Sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, chorioretinal lesions, or optic atrophy in onchocerciasis (impending/established blindness) (Harrison 22e p.1823)
High Loa loa microfilaremia (>30,000 microfilariae/mL): risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy with ivermectin or DEC (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823)
Loiasis with CNS involvement during treatment of heavy microfilaremia (coma, encephalitis) (Harrison 22e p.1823)
Chyluria from retroperitoneal lymphatic obstruction in lymphatic filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1820)
Progressive interstitial pulmonary fibrosis in untreated TPE (Harrison 22e p.1822)
harrison.prognosis: Filarial infections are chronic with potential long-term debilitating effects; adult worms live for many years (W. bancrofti/Brugia >2 decades; O. volvulus up to ~18 years, average ~9). Most microfilaremic persons remain clinically asymptomatic for years, and only a minority progress to acute or chronic disease, but lymphatic damage can become permanent (elephantiasis, hydrocele). In onchocerciasis, visual loss is the most serious outcome and blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold increased mortality. Loiasis, historically considered relatively benign in endemic populations, is now linked to chronic morbidity and increased mortality. TPE responds to therapy but relapses in ~12-25% of cases (sometimes years later); untreated TPE can progress to pulmonary fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823).
pitfalls: Seropositivity (antifilarial antibody) cannot be equated with active infection; endemic residents can become sensitized via mosquito exposure without patent infection (Harrison 22e p.1821).
Antifilarial antibody/antigen serology has extensive cross-reactivity with other helminths; W. bancrofti antigen tests can be falsely positive in Loa loa infection (Harrison 22e p.1821).
Many infected individuals are amicrofilaremic, and travelers are often amicrofilaremic, so a negative blood smear does not exclude filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821, 1823).
Timing of blood collection to the local microfilarial periodicity is critical; mistimed samples miss nocturnally or diurnally periodic microfilariae (Harrison 22e p.1821).
DLA is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820).
Eosinophilia and elevated IgE are nonspecific (common to many parasitic infections) and are not diagnostic by themselves (Harrison 22e p.1823).
For every palpable onchocercal nodule there are an estimated four deeper nonpalpable ones (Harrison 22e p.1823).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison describes lymphatic filariasis along a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading: asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL)/dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema progressing to elephantiasis). Onchocerciasis severity is gauged by infection burden (skin/eye involvement increasing with moderate-to-heavy microfilarial load). Loa loa microfilaremia is stratified by treatment risk, with >30,000 microfilariae/mL marking high risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy (Harrison 22e p.1820-1823).
management: Antifilarial chemotherapy tailored to species: diethylcarbamazine for bancroftian and brugian lymphatic filariasis, and ivermectin with albendazole for onchocerciasis
Doxycycline to target the Wolbachia endosymbiont, giving sustained reduction in adult-worm viability and microfilariae
Careful pre-treatment assessment of Loa loa microfilarial load before ivermectin or diethylcarbamazine, given the risk of treatment-related encephalopathy in heavy loiasis
Lymphoedema and elephantiasis care with meticulous skin hygiene, limb elevation, compression and prompt treatment of secondary bacterial infection to limit acute adenolymphangitis
Surgical management of hydrocele and genital lymphatic disease
Prevention through vector control and community mass drug administration in endemic areas
Referral to infectious diseases or tropical medicine and to lymphoedema specialists for chronic disease
